title: Mastery Challenge: Probability & Statistics
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Probability & Statistics Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: One question from each chapter: percents, spread, chance, bets, risk, polls, experiments, charts, traps and the news. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Probability & Statistics Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Ten questions from across the tree, from your first percent to the numbers in the news. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Probability & Statistics: mastered
learned: How to question any statistic: of what, compared to what, from whom, and how sure.
Why a fair sample, a control group and chance assignment make evidence worth trusting.
How chance, expected value and base rates explain casinos, streaks and false positives.
Why a chart, an extreme result or an algorithm's verdict needs the real data behind it.

questions.prompt: A share price starts at $200, falls 50% on Monday and rises 50% on Tuesday, ending up at _____.

options.rationale: That's after Monday's fall only.
The rise is taken from the smaller, fallen price.
Each percent is measured from its own start.

questions.explanation: Down 50% takes $200 to $100; up 50% of $100 adds only $50, so it ends at $150.

questions.prompt: Two classes both average 6 out of 10 on a quiz. Class A's standard deviation is about 1; Class B's is about 3. What does that tell you?

options.label: Class B did better, since its number is bigger
options.rationale: Both have the same mean; this number measures spread, not level.

options.label: Class A had three times as many students
options.rationale: It says nothing about how many took the quiz.

options.label: Class B's scores sit further from the average
Every score in Class A was exactly 6
options.rationale: Then its standard deviation would be zero, not about 1.

questions.explanation: The standard deviation is the typical distance from the mean. Same center, but Class B's scores are about three times as scattered.

questions.prompt: A fair coin lands heads 7 times in its first 10 tosses. Why will the share of heads probably be close to 50% after 1,000 tosses?

options.label: The early lead gets swamped by the later tosses
Tails will come up more often to pay back the lead
options.rationale: Coins keep no score: luck is swamped, not repaid.

options.label: A coin tossed often wears down and becomes fair
options.rationale: It was fair all along; the share just settles.

options.label: The first ten tosses stop counting after a while
options.rationale: They still count; they just matter less and less.

questions.explanation: Few tries swing, many settle. Three extra heads barely move the share after 1,000 tosses, even though nothing pays them back.

questions.prompt: In the Monty Hall puzzle, the host shows a goat and two doors are left. Why does switching win 2 times in 3?

options.label: The host opens one of the doors completely at random
options.rationale: He knows where the car is, and always shows a goat.

options.label: The car is placed more often behind the middle door
options.rationale: The car's place is random; the host's choice isn't.

options.label: Two doors left always means a 50/50 choice
options.rationale: Only if the host chose at random; he knowingly shows a goat.

options.label: Your first pick is a goat 2 times in 3

questions.explanation: Your first pick is the car only 1 time in 3. The other 2 times, the host must show the other goat, so the door he leaves shut hides the car.

questions.prompt: The same 90% accurate test is used where 1 in 100 people have a condition and where 1 in 10 do. Why is a positive far likelier to be real in the second place?

options.label: False alarms from healthy people no longer swamp the true cases
Its sensitivity rises when a condition is more common
options.rationale: Sensitivity is 90% in both places; the base rate changed.

options.label: A common condition is easier for a lab to spot
options.rationale: The test's accuracy is the same in both places.

options.label: People in the second place are tested twice
options.rationale: Nothing says so; the base rate is what changed.

questions.explanation: At 1 in 100, 990 false alarms swamp 90 true cases: 1 in 12 positives is real. At 1 in 10, it's 900 true against 900 false: 1 in 2.

questions.prompt: In 1936 the Literary Digest got about 2.4 million answers and still picked the wrong winner. Why didn't the huge sample save it?

options.label: It counted the ballots too slowly to call the race
options.rationale: Timing wasn't the problem; who was on the list was.

options.label: Polls of over a million people stop being accurate
options.rationale: Size doesn't hurt; it just can't fix bias.

options.label: Voters changed their minds after it was published
options.rationale: A 1988 study traced it to a biased sample and biased replies.

options.label: Its names came from lists that leaned toward better-off voters

questions.explanation: A bigger sample shrinks chance error, not bias. Phone and car lists in the Depression gave the wrong mix of people, so more answers just gave the wrong answer more confidently.

questions.prompt: A study reports p = 0.05. Which reading of that p-value is right?

options.label: Such results would be rare if nothing were going on
There is a 5% chance the finding is a fluke
options.rationale: The classic misreading the ASA warned against in 2016.

options.label: There is a 95% chance the finding is true
options.rationale: A p-value is not the chance the finding is true.

options.label: The effect is big enough to matter in real life
options.rationale: Significant doesn't mean big; ask for the effect size.

questions.explanation: A p-value asks how surprising results this striking would be if nothing were going on. It is not the chance the finding is true or a fluke.

questions.prompt: A bar chart shows sales of 100 and 105 on an axis starting at 95, so the second bar looks twice as tall. What is the real rise?

options.label: About double, as the bars show
options.rationale: The axis starts at 95, so the bars exaggerate the gap.

options.label: About 50%
options.rationale: Divide the change, 5, by the start, 100.
10 is how tall the second bar is drawn, not the rise.

questions.explanation: The change is 5 on a start of 100: 5 ÷ 100 is a 5% rise. Starting the axis at 95 draws the bars 5 and 10 units tall, so a small gap looks like a doubling.

questions.prompt: A town puts speed cameras at the junctions with the most crashes last year, and crashes there fall. What fair test would show whether the cameras did it?

options.label: Count crashes at the same junctions for another year
options.rationale: Still before and after; the drift back toward average continues.

options.label: Randomly give cameras to half the worst junctions, then compare
Ask drivers whether the cameras made them slow down
options.rationale: Opinions can't separate the cameras from the drift back to average.

options.label: Put cameras at the safest junctions instead
options.rationale: Those drift too, just the other way.

questions.explanation: Junctions picked at their worst drift back toward average anyway. Splitting them by chance means both groups drift alike, so only the difference shows what the cameras did.

questions.prompt: Amazon's hiring tool marked down résumés containing the word "women's". Much like the 1936 Literary Digest poll, what was the root cause?

options.label: Engineers deliberately told it to prefer male applicants
options.rationale: Nobody programmed that; it learned it from data.

options.label: It had far too few résumés to learn anything from
options.rationale: It had 10 years' worth; as with the Digest, size didn't fix the mix.

options.label: It was only ever tested on the wrong kinds of jobs
options.rationale: The problem was in its training data.

options.label: It learned from 10 years of résumés, mostly from men

questions.explanation: An algorithm learns the patterns in its data, including unfair ones: bias in, bias out. As with the Digest's lists, more tilted data just repeats the tilt.
